title: Looking back: the thought

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the streams and the places, and the same Granth opened at the center of them. Your line was many streams. Which place did you find yourself walking into? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

At the end of a long course, a student is handed a blank card and one instruction: in a single sentence, what did you learn? It can be harder than the exam. For a long block this year, the path put four big questions to the Granth. What is God like? Who am I, really? How should I live? And what is this world? A few days ago we walked back through all of it at speed. Today we go slower: one line of the Granth for each question, held up and looked at, and then the blank card comes to you.
screen: `ONE BLANK CARD.` → `FOUR QUESTIONS.` → `ONE LINE FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: God first. In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan holds two things together. In paraphrase: He Himself is beyond all qualities, and He is with qualities too. Beyond every form, and present in every form. The hymns keep both halves. That's why the Granth can call God formless on one page and Beloved, Friend and Husband on the next. Then the self. In the Asa di Var, a salok of Guru Angad names the trouble plainly. In paraphrase: ego is a long, deep illness, and the medicine is found within it too. Haumai, the I that keeps grabbing the center, isn't the whole of a person. The same self that grabs can learn to let go. Then ethics, how to live. Elsewhere in the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak gives a short line that carries a whole ethic. In paraphrase: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of every virtue and every good. Not a long list of rules. Two plain qualities, kept in the voice and in the way a person stands among others. And the world. At the close of the Japji, the final salok says, in paraphrase: air is the Guru, water the father, and the great earth the mother. The world isn't a waiting room. It's family, and it teaches. Put the four together and you have a shape. One God, with qualities and beyond them. A self that is sick with ego and can be healed. A life measured by sweetness and humility. A world that is kin. It all arrives as poetry, much of it sung, and that matters. Sikh thought isn't a form to sign. It's a set of lines to carry, and to keep turning over.
screen: `GOD: BEYOND QUALITIES, AND WITH THEM.` · `SELF: EGO, AND ITS MEDICINE.` · `ETHICS: SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · `WORLD: AIR THE GURU, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · then, large: `LINES TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your key idea. Settle, and breathe. Suppose a friend asked you tonight, over tea, what the Gurus teach. Not what the books say about it: what you would say. Let today's four lines go by once, slowly. Beyond qualities, and with them. Ego, and its medicine. Sweetness and humility. Air the Guru, earth the mother. Then wait for your own sentence to form, in a few plain words. Not a summary of the Gurus. Just where you stand today. If nothing comes, that's an answer too. If you pray, you can bring the question itself into the prayer. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today, at Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world, each held in a line of the Granth. Today's word.
Your line: what I think now. Today, write your key idea down in one sentence and put the date beside it, so a later you can see where you stood. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs learn the Gurus' thought by hearing and singing the Granth's hymns and through katha, the spoken explanation of a hymn, often returning to lines like the Mool Mantar and the close of the Japji.

myth: in the Japji's closing salok, the world is only a waiting room
it calls air the Guru, water the father, and the great earth the mother.

in the Asa di Var: sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue and every good.
the Gurus call God only formless

fork.setup: a salok of Guru Angad names ego a long, deep illness. where does he say the medicine is?
options: within the same place as the illness.
fork.reveal: in the Asa di Var: ego is a deep illness, and the medicine is found within it too.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nirgun, beyond qualities; the Sukhmani says God is nirgun and sargun, with qualities, too.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikh thought is a list of beliefs to sign.
what it means: the Gurus answer four big questions, about God, the self, how to live and the world, in lines of the Granth.
what a scholar hears: the thought arrives as poetry, much of it set to raga, so it is meant to be sung and carried, not only stated.
recall: the will, arriving in a life

notes: Look-back day for Block G (Sikh thought, days 1362–1419), organized by the outline's four headings: God, self, ethics, world.
Please confirm the Angs and paraphrases: Ang 287 (nirgun aap sargun bhee ohee, Sukhmani), Ang 466 (haumai deeragh rog hai, daaroo bhee is maahi), Ang 8 (pavan guroo paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat).
The Ang 466 haumai salok is attributed here to Guru Angad (Mahala 2) within Guru Nanak's Asa di Var; please confirm.
The Japji's closing salok is attributed by some to Guru Nanak and by others to Guru Angad; the script says only 'the final salok'.

Editor pass: day 1419 opened its walk-back with Ik Onkar and ran the same four rooms in its practice, and day 1417 taught 'truth is high, but higher still is truthful living' with a myth item on it. So the hook (now a blank-card image, naming the earlier walk-back), the ethics line (now Ang 470, mithat neevee, from day 1395), the practice (now a friend's question over tea), two myth items, a match pair, the original (now ਨਿਰਗੁਣ) and the sources were changed; 'the Gurus never let either half go' was softened to 'the hymns keep both halves'.
